beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Surya, and this video is about the database behind a Canvas integration. Eleven tables, what each one is for, and a count that looked like a mistake and was not.

show.event: title snaps in, signal rule above, mono subtitle THE LTI SCHEMA

beats.narration_text: The schema does three jobs, and nothing else. It remembers who is allowed to launch. It maps Canvas's idea of a person onto ours. And it forgets things, on a timer, on purpose.

show.event: three full-width bands snap in, the third in signal

beats.narration_text: Two tables answer the first. Platform registrations holds every Canvas instance we trust: its client identifier, its issuer, where it publishes its keys. Deployments holds the specific installation inside that instance. Together they are the guest list. A launch from something not in these tables is not a launch. It is a stranger.

show.event: two bordered table cards side by side, then the signal line beneath

beats.narration_text: Three tables answer the second. User links maps a Canvas subject identifier to a user in our system. Course links maps a Canvas course to ours. Resource links maps the specific thing that was clicked. Which means we do not store a Canvas person at all. We store a correspondence between two identifiers.

show.event: three CANVAS SIDE to OUR SIDE rows with separate arrowheads

beats.narration_text: Two tables exist in order to forget. The nonce store holds the one-time values from a login, for ten minutes. Launch sessions holds the audit record of a launch, for one hour. Then both are purged. A table whose job is to expire is doing security work, not bookkeeping.

show.event: two countdown cards, durations large in signal, THEN PURGED beneath

beats.narration_text: Three more carry the older protocol: credentials, nonces and launches for LTI one point one. The same three shapes, an older handshake, kept for platforms that have not moved yet.

show.event: three mono rows in mute, set back from the others

beats.narration_text: Which brings us to a number that looked like an error. Our working notes said ten tables. The security review said eleven. Both were correct. Ten tables carry the LTI prefix. Eleven have row level security switched on: those ten, plus the institutions table, which belongs to the same schema but is not prefixed. The count depended on whether you were counting names, or counting protections.

show.event: two large numerals with mono captions, plus institutions between them

beats.narration_text: Row level security is on all eleven, restricted to the backend service role, and a non-service role is denied both reads and writes. The schema is small deliberately. Every table it does not have is a table that cannot leak.

show.event: RLS 11/11 full width, then a hard cut to the title restated
